pll1d2c4-d1e3473.summary: Announces the plan of citing Old and New Testament authorities to demonstrate the truth of divine unity and Trinity.

pll1d2c4-d1e3476.summary: Cites Deut 6:4, 'Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one God,' as the first witness to divine unity.
claims: God is one.

pll1d2c4-d1e3491.summary: Cites the First Commandment's prohibition of other gods as a further witness to divine unity.
claims: There are no other gods besides the Lord.

pll1d2c4-d1e3503.summary: Glosses the preceding texts: they signify the unity of the divine nature, since, per Ambrose, 'God' and 'Lord' are names of nature and power.
claims: 'God' and 'Lord' name nature and power.

pll1d2c4-d1e3528.summary: Reads Exod 3:14 grammatically: God says 'I am,' not 'we are,' and 'He who is,' not 'who are,' showing that there is only one God.
claims: The singular in 'I am who am' shows there is one God.

pll1d2c4-d1e3549.summary: From the Song of Exodus, notes the singular 'his name' ('the Lord, almighty is his name'), not 'name of Lords,' as signifying unity.
claims: The singular name signifies divine unity.

pll1d2c4-d1e3570.summary: Interprets Gen 1:26 as showing both: 'let us make' and 'our' indicate plurality of persons, while 'image' indicates unity of essence.
claims: 'Let us make' and 'our' show plurality of persons.
'Image' shows unity of essence.

pll1d2c4-d1e3594.summary: Confirms the reading of Gen 1:26 with the De fide ad Petrum: a single person would not say 'our'; 'image' shows one nature in whose image man is made.
claims: If there were only one person, Scripture would not say 'our image.'
One image implies one nature.

pll1d2c4-d1e3628.summary: Adds Hilary: Gen 1:26 shows that in the Trinity there is neither diversity nor singularity or solitude, but likeness and plurality, since an image is not alone and likeness excludes diversity.
claims: In the Trinity there is neither diversity nor solitude.
There is likeness and plurality or distinction.

pll1d2c4-d1e3659.summary: Gives Hilary's longer argument: the plural 'let us make' and 'our' profess a partnership (consortium) that excludes solitude, while the common image excludes diversity. So the confession must be of a God neither solitary nor diverse.
claims: Plural speech excludes solitude in God.
A common image and likeness excludes diversity of divinity.
God must be confessed as neither solitary nor diverse.

pll1d2c4-d1e3700.summary: Lombard's interpretive principle drawn from Hilary: the term 'partnership' or 'plurality' of persons posits nothing in God but removes something, namely solitude and singularity; 'several persons' means 'not one alone.'
claims: Terms of plurality in God remove rather than posit.
To say there are several persons is to say there is not one alone.

pll1d2c4-d1e3708.summary: Develops the remotive reading: 'three persons' excludes that any person, or any pair, is alone. Defers to later distinctions the questions of how the persons are 'similar' and whether there is diversity or difference among them.
claims: Saying 'three persons' excludes the solitude of any one person or pair.
How the persons are alike and whether they differ will be treated later.

pll1d2c4-d1e3723.summary: Returns to the main thread: further authorities will be adduced for plurality of persons and unity of essence.

pll1d2c4-d1e3726.summary: Reads Gen 1:1 Trinitarianly, with 'God' as Father and 'beginning' as Son, and notes that the Hebrew Elohim, plural of El, refers to the plurality of persons.
claims: 'In the beginning' signifies the Son.
The plural Elohim indicates plurality of persons.

pll1d2c4-d1e3755.summary: Adds the serpent's 'you shall be as gods' (Gen 3:5), where Hebrew Elohim is read as 'divine persons.'
claims: Elohim in Gen 3:5 refers to the divine persons.

pll1d2c4-d1e3770.summary: Cites David's 'the Lord is his name' (Ps 67:5), singular rather than 'of Lords,' to show the unity of the divine nature.
claims: The singular divine name shows unity of nature.

pll1d2c4-d1e3795.summary: Interprets Ps 80:9–10 with Ambrose: 'no new god' shows eternity and 'no alien god' shows unity of substance, so Son and Spirit are neither later than the Father nor of another divinity, being born of and proceeding from him.
claims: Son and Holy Spirit are not posterior to the Father.
Son and Holy Spirit are not of another divinity.
The Son is born of the Father; the Spirit proceeds from the Father.

pll1d2c4-d1e3825.summary: Reads Ps 32:6 ('by the Word of the Lord... by the Spirit of his mouth') as suggesting the distinction of persons.
claims: Ps 32:6 suggests the Word and Spirit as distinct persons.

pll1d2c4-d1e3837.summary: Reads Ps 66 with Abelard: the threefold 'God' expresses the trinity of persons, and the singular 'him' expresses the unity of essence.
claims: Threefold naming expresses three persons; the singular pronoun expresses one essence.

pll1d2c4-d1e3854.summary: Reads the Seraphim's threefold 'Holy' (Isa 6:3) as signifying the Trinity and 'Lord God' as signifying the unity of essence.
claims: The Trisagion signifies the Trinity.
'Lord God' signifies unity of essence.

pll1d2c4-d1e3876.summary: Cites Ps 2:7 ('You are my Son, today I have begotten you') as a clear indication of the eternal generation of the Son.
claims: Ps 2:7 speaks of the Son's eternal generation.

pll1d2c4-d1e3890.summary: Cites Isa 53:8 ('who shall declare his generation?') as referring to the ineffable generation.
claims: The generation of the Son is ineffable.

pll1d2c4-d1e3906.summary: Cites Prov 8:22–30, where Wisdom speaks of being conceived and brought forth before creation, as plain witness to the Son's eternal generation and coexistence with the Father.
claims: Wisdom was begotten before the world.
The Son exists eternally with the Father.

pll1d2c4-d1e3920.summary: Adds Sir 24:5, Wisdom 'came forth from the mouth of the Most High, firstborn before all creatures.'
claims: Wisdom is begotten before all creation.

pll1d2c4-d1e3932.summary: Reads Micah 5:2 as indicating both the eternal generation of the Word ('from the days of eternity') and his temporal birth from Mary in Bethlehem.
claims: Micah 5:2 refers to both the eternal and temporal generation of the Word.

pll1d2c4-d1e3946.summary: Announces express Old Testament testimonies to the Holy Spirit.
claims: The Old Testament witnesses to the Holy Spirit.

pll1d2c4-d1e3949.summary: Cites Gen 1:2, 'the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters.'
claims: The Spirit of the Lord appears at creation.

pll1d2c4-d1e3964.summary: Cites Ps 138:7, 'Where shall I go from your Spirit?'
claims: Scripture speaks of the Spirit of God.

pll1d2c4-d1e3982.summary: Cites Wis 1:5–6 on the holy Spirit of discipline and the kindly spirit of wisdom.
claims: Scripture names the Holy Spirit.

pll1d2c4-d1e3999.summary: Cites Isa 61:1, 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,' completing the Old Testament witness to the Spirit.
claims: Scripture names the Spirit of the Lord.

pl-l1d2c4.summary: Assembles Old Testament testimonies to the unity of the divine nature and the plurality of persons. Texts such as the Shema, the First Commandment, 'I am who am,' and 'the Lord is his name' show unity; Genesis 1:26 ('let us make... our image'), read with Augustine and Hilary, shows both plurality and unity. Lombard draws out Hilary's point that number terms in God remove solitude rather than posit something. Further texts point to the persons: Elohim, the Psalms, the threefold Sanctus, the eternal generation of the Son (Ps 2, Prov 8, Sir 24, Micah 5), and the Holy Spirit (Gen 1:2, Ps 138, Wis 1, Isa 61).
claims: The Old Testament attests the unity of the divine nature.
Genesis 1:26 shows both plurality of persons ('let us make', 'our') and unity of essence ('image').
Terms of plurality in God remove singularity and solitude rather than positing something.
Scripture witnesses to the eternal generation of the Son.
The Old Testament contains express testimonies to the Holy Spirit.
concepts: Holy Spirit in the Old Testament
